title: Snakes - progressive enhancer decay, and a bud that is still there
mechanism: Snake limb loss is not one event. In basal snakes (boa, python) the ZRS is ~80% identical to limbed lizards and still has detectable ZPA activity in boa; in advanced snakes the substitution rate jumps and ZPA activity is gone; in corn snake no ZRS sequence was detected at all. Crucially the python hindlimb bud still initiates, and its HOXD digit enhancers are conserved - the bud reaches a distal phase with transient pre-chondrogenic condensations of tibia, fibula and footplate before arresting.
intervention: Not an intervention - nature's. The engineering lesson is that limb loss was achieved in stages, and that the cis-regulatory decay appears to have STARTED WITH OR AFTER other disruptive events, not before them.
predicted_phenotype: Advanced snakes: complete absence of all skeletal limb structures. Basal snakes: vestigial pelvic girdle and rudimentary hindlimbs. Python embryo: hindlimb development arrests; apical-ridge and polarizing-region signalling pathways are not activated; SHH is weak and transient.

evidence.finding: Advanced-snake ZRS shows a substantially increased substitution rate; ZRS from rattlesnake and cobra 'completely lost ZPA-specific activity'; only boa retained ZPA activity; 'The only snake genome in which no ZRS sequence was detected belonged to the corn snake.' And: 'we do not expect that the reintroduction of a fully functional ZRS into a snake genome alone would be sufficient to induce the formation of fully or even partially developed limbs in snakes.'

evidence.cite: Cohn MJ & Tickle C 1999, Nature 399:474-9, 'Developmental basis of limblessness and axial patterning in snakes'
evidence.finding: 'Hindlimb buds are initiated, but apical-ridge and polarizing-region signalling pathways that are normally required for limb development are not activated. Leg bud outgrowth and signalling by Sonic hedgehog in pythons can be rescued by application of fibroblast growth factor or by recombination with chick apical ridge.' Hox expression domains are expanded along the body axis, accounting for forelimb absence and thoracic expansion.

evidence.cite: Leal F & Cohn MJ 2016, Curr Biol 26:2966-73, 'Loss and Re-emergence of Legs in Snakes by Modular Evolution of Sonic hedgehog and HOXD Enhancers'
evidence.finding: 'hindlimb development arrests in python embryos as a result of mutations that abolish essential transcription factor binding sites in the limb-specific enhancer of Sonic hedgehog (SHH). Consequently, SHH transcription is weak and transient'. HOXD digit enhancers are conserved; buds form transitory pre-chondrogenic condensations of tibia, fibula and footplate.

reversibility: The most important negative result in the whole design space: Cohn & Tickle showed python leg bud outgrowth and SHH signalling CAN be rescued by an FGF bead or a chick apical ridge - so the mesenchyme is still competent. But Kvon et al. explicitly expect that restoring the ZRS alone would NOT restore limbs in a snake, because other changes must also have occurred. Rescuable in an embryo manipulation; not rescuable by one genomic edit.
specificity: Whole-lineage; forelimb loss in snakes is attributed to expanded axial Hox domains, a different mechanism from the hindlimb ZRS lesion. Two mechanisms in one animal.
difficulty: Not applicable; this is comparative evidence.
what_we_would_run: The ZRS ortholog series across 16 species IS the benchmark dataset, and it is the one piece of this subject that maps directly onto what a genome language model emits a score for. We have not scored it.
open_questions: Forelimb loss (Hox-mediated) and hindlimb reduction (ZRS-mediated) are different mechanisms in the same animal. Any single-locus account of 'the gene for snake limblessness' is incomplete by the field's own statement.

title: Limb-reduced lizards - the knob is how LONG SHH is on, and the losses are not all the same
mechanism: In the Australian skink genus Hemiergis, closely related populations differ in digit number, and evolutionary digit loss is NOT a simple truncation of a pentadactyl programme. The duration of embryonic SHH expression is shortened in limbs with fewer digits, correlating with decreased posterior cell proliferation. Expression of MSX and Distal-less proteins is similar between populations, so the change is specific rather than a general developmental slowdown.
intervention: Not an intervention. The engineering translation is the Shh-duration knob, which in mouse is exactly the ShhCreER timing route.
predicted_phenotype: Graded digit reduction tracking SHH duration. Different squamate clades reduce differently: in Brachymeles, digit-number variation suggests a more labile Digit V than Digit I, contrary to Morse's law and different from Lerista, Hemiergis and Carlia - 'the first evidence of clade-specific modes of digit reduction'.

evidence.cite: Shapiro MD, Hanken J & Rosenthal N 2003, J Exp Zool B 297:48-56, 'Developmental basis of evolutionary digit loss in the Australian lizard Hemiergis'
evidence.finding: 'the duration of embryonic expression of the patterning molecule Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is shortened in limbs with reduced numbers of digits, and is correlated with decreased cell proliferation in the posterior aspect of the limb ... expression of MSX and Distal-less proteins were similar among embryos from different populations.'

evidence.cite: Wagner GP et al. 2018, J Morphol 279:1104-1119, 'Are there general laws for digit evolution in squamates? The loss and re-evolution of digits in a clade of fossorial lizards (Brachymeles, Scincinae)'
evidence.finding: Strong statistical support for digit, but not limb, re-evolution in Brachymeles. 'Digit number variation suggests a more labile Digit V than Digit I, contrary to Morse's law. The observed pattern of digit variation is different from that of other scincid lizards (Lerista, Hemiergis, Carlia) ... the first evidence of clade-specific modes of digit reduction.'

evidence.cite: Rabosky DL et al. 2014, Syst Biol 63:610-27, 'Analysis and visualization of complex macroevolutionary dynamics: an example from Australian scincid lizards'
evidence.finding: 'The Lerista clade is characterized by relatively high lability of body form and has undergone repeated instances of limb reduction.'

evidence.cite: Camaiti M et al. 2024, Proc Biol Sci 291:20241653, 'Patterns of girdle shape and their correlates in Australian limb-reduced skinks'
evidence.finding: Geometric morphometrics across 90 limb-reduced skink species and limbed relatives: clavicle shape converges on an acute anterior bend when forelimbs are lost but hindlimbs retained; coracoid and pelvis simplify as undulation replaces limbed locomotion; girdle integration decreases in taxa lacking forelimb but not hindlimb elements.

reversibility: Wagner et al. report statistical support for DIGIT re-evolution but not limb re-evolution in Brachymeles - the clearest comparative statement available on whether this is reversible on evolutionary timescales.
specificity: Clade-specific, and that is the finding: there is no single squamate mechanism of limb reduction.
what_we_would_run: Nothing. This route is on the page to refute the framing that there is 'a' mechanism for limb loss. Four independent squamate radiations reduce limbs by at least partly different routes, and that is the empirical case for presenting a DESIGN SPACE rather than an answer.
open_questions: We found NO molecular (sequence or expression) mechanism published for Lerista limb reduction - the most-cited example of repeated limb loss. Our searches covered 'Lerista limb reduction skink evolution' on PubMed and returned four records, all taxonomic, morphometric or macroevolutionary. That is the scope of our negative; we did not search non-English sources, theses, or preprint servers.

The Camaiti girdle result raises a question we cannot answer: is the converged clavicle shape a locomotor adaptation or a developmental consequence of forelimb loss? The authors give both as possibilities.

title: Whales and dolphins - the bud forms, the AER forms, and then nothing maintains it
mechanism: Cetacean embryos DO initiate hindlimb buds; in dolphins the bud arrests and degenerates around the fifth gestational week. The hindlimb bud forms an AER and expresses Fgf8 initially, but neither the AER nor Fgf8 expression is maintained. SHH is absent from the bud, and the failure to establish a ZPA is associated with absence of HAND2, an upstream regulator of SHH. Separately, cetacean ZRS reporter activity is significantly lower than mouse, consistent with cessation of hindlimb-bud SHH.
intervention: Not an intervention. The translated design is a maintenance failure, not an induction failure - the mouse analogue is beta-catenin removal after AER induction, or late AER-FGF inactivation.
predicted_phenotype: Complete hindlimb loss in the adult; a transient, arrested bud in the embryo. Thewissen et al. interpret the fossil and developmental records together: reduction of SHH expression around 41 Ma led to loss of distal elements, and total loss of SHH expression near the origin of the modern suborders around 34 Ma accounts for further loss - with hindlimb SIZE reduced earlier by gradual microevolutionary change, long before the developmental genes changed.

evidence.finding: 'In dolphins, the bud arrests and degenerates around the fifth gestational week ... the cetacean hind-limb bud forms an AER and ... this structure expresses Fgf8 initially, but ... neither the AER nor Fgf8 expression is maintained. Moreover, Sonic hedgehog (Shh) ... is absent ... failure to establish a ZPA is associated with the absence of Hand2.' 'Long after locomotor function was totally lost, modulation of developmental control genes eliminated most of the hind-limb skeleton.'

evidence.cite: Sun L et al. 2022, BMC Genomics 23:797, 'Evolutionary genetics of flipper forelimb and hindlimb loss from limb development-related genes in cetaceans'
evidence.finding: 'the regulatory activity of the SHH gene enhancer-ZRS in cetaceans-was significantly lower than in mice, which is consistent with the cessation of SHH gene expression in the hindlimb bud'; accelerated evolution of TBX5 on ancestral cetacean branches; a parallel/convergent FGF10 site (D42G) and a rapidly evolving GREM1 CNE in marine mammals.

evidence.cite: Gavazzi LM et al. 2024, Dev Dyn 253:859-874, 'Protein signaling and morphological development of the tail fluke in the embryonic beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas)'
evidence.finding: In a beluga embryo, immunohistochemistry showed epidermal WNT and FGF signals and mesenchymal/epidermal SHH and GREMLIN in the developing tail fluke, 'most consistent with vertebrate limb development' - i.e. the limb programme was redeployed in a novel appendage after the hindlimb was lost. Single case study; authors state further work is required.

reversibility: Not applicable, but the beluga fluke result is the striking counterpoint: the limb-outgrowth signalling programme was not lost from the genome, it was redeployed elsewhere in the body.
specificity: Hindlimb only - forelimbs became flippers with webbed digits and hyperphalangy, a gain-of-structure change in the same animal.
what_we_would_run: Nothing, but this is the strongest comparative argument for the MAINTENANCE class of routes: the one natural limb loss where we know the AER formed and then failed is also the one where loss is complete. If you want a limbless animal rather than a truncated one, removing maintenance may beat blocking induction.
open_questions: Thewissen et al. report an ASSOCIATION between absent HAND2 and failure to establish a ZPA. We read the abstract; we would not restate it as causation.
The 41 Ma and 34 Ma dates are the authors' integration of fossil and developmental data, i.e. their inference, not a measurement.

title: Stickleback pelvic loss - the cleanest natural proof that cis-regulation is the viable route
mechanism: Threespine stickleback populations have repeatedly lost the pelvic apparatus, the hindlimb homologue, through deletion of a tissue-specific Pitx1 enhancer. The same gene's null allele is lethal in laboratory animals. So evolution reached the phenotype by removing the gene's expression in one tissue rather than removing the gene - the same logic as the ZRS, in an independent lineage and a different gene.
intervention: Not an intervention. It is the design precedent that the whole cis-regulatory half of this page rests on.
predicted_phenotype: Pelvic (hindlimb-homologue) reduction or loss, viable, with molecular signatures of positive selection in pelvic-reduced populations.

evidence.finding: 'Pelvic loss in different natural populations of threespine stickleback fish has occurred through regulatory mutations deleting a tissue-specific enhancer of the Pituitary homeobox transcription factor 1 (Pitx1) gene. The high prevalence of deletion mutations at Pitx1 may be influenced by inherent structural features of the locus. Although Pitx1 null mutations are lethal in laboratory animals, Pitx1 regulatory mutations show molecular signatures of positive selection in pelvic-reduced populations.'

reversibility: Recurrent in both directions across populations; the locus's structural fragility makes the deletion repeatable, which is itself the mechanism of the repeatability.
lethality_risk: None - these are wild, reproducing fish.
what_we_would_run: Two independent natural experiments (stickleback Pitx1, snake ZRS) converge on the same engineering principle: to remove an appendage without killing the animal, delete a tissue-specific enhancer, not the gene. That principle is the page's single transferable conclusion, and it is supported by evidence from two phyla rather than by our opinion.
open_questions: Does the equivalent mouse Pitx1 hindlimb enhancer exist and is it single or redundant? See mol-pitx1-hindlimb-enhancer; unknown to us.
